Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: $$(5x+3)^2=(\sqrt{3x+7})^2\Rightarrow25x^2+30x+9=3x+7\Rightarrow25x^2+27x+2=0\Rightarrow x=\frac{-27\pm\sqrt{27^2-4(25)(2)}}{50}=\frac{-27\pm23}{50}\Rightarrow x=-1\text{ or }x=-\tfrac{2}{25}.$$ Checking both in the original, only $$x=-\tfrac{2}{25}$$ satisfies the equation.

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_title: Solve the following equations using the quadratic formula.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Use the quadratic formula $$x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$$ for each equation and simplify the surds where possible.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: $$(a)\ a=1,b=3,c=1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt{9-4}}{2}=\dfrac{-3\pm\sqrt5}{2}.$$ $$(b)\ a=1,b=-3,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{9+8}}{2}=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{17}}{2}.$$ $$(c)\ a=1,b=6,c=6\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{36-24}}{2}=\dfrac{-6\pm\sqrt{12}}{2}=-3\pm\sqrt3.$$ $$(d)\ a=1,b=-5,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{25+8}}{2}=\dfrac{5\pm\sqrt{33}}{2}.$$ $$(e)\ a=3,b=10,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-10\pm\sqrt{100+24}}{6}=\dfrac{-10\pm\sqrt{124}}{6}=\dfrac{-10\pm2\sqrt{31}}{6}=\dfrac{-5\pm\sqrt{31}}{3}.$$ $$(f)\ a=4,b=-4,c=-1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{16+16}}{8}=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{32}}{8}=\dfrac{4\pm4\sqrt2}{8}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt2}{2}.$$ $$(g)\ 4x^{2}-7x-2=0,\ a=4,b=-7,c=-2\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{49+32}}{8}=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{81}}{8}=\dfrac{7\pm9}{8}\Rightarrow x=2,\ -\tfrac14.$$ $$(h)\ a=11,b=2,c=-7\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{4+308}}{22}=\dfrac{-2\pm\sqrt{312}}{22}=\dfrac{-2\pm2\sqrt{78}}{22}=\dfrac{-1\pm\sqrt{78}}{11}.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Solve the following equations using the quadratic formula. Give your answers to three significant figures: (a) $$x^{2}+4x+2=0$$ (b) $$x^{2}-8x+1=0$$ (c) $$x^{2}+11x-9=0$$ (d) $$x^{2}-7x-17=0$$ (e) $$5x^{2}+9x-1=0$$ (f) $$2x^{2}-3x-18=0$$ (g) $$3x^{2}+8=16x$$ (h) $$2x^{2}+11x=5x^{2}-18$$.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Apply $$x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$$ to each, then evaluate the roots numerically and round to 3 s.f.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: $$(a)\ a=1,b=4,c=2\Rightarrow x=-2\pm\sqrt2\Rightarrow x\approx-0.586,-3.41.$$ $$(b)\ a=1,b=-8,c=1\Rightarrow x=4\pm\sqrt{15}\Rightarrow x\approx7.87,0.127.$$ $$(c)\ a=1,b=11,c=-9\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-11\pm\sqrt{157}}{2}\Rightarrow x\approx0.765,-11.8.$$ $$(d)\ a=1,b=-7,c=-17\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{117}}{2}\Rightarrow x\approx8.91,-1.91.$$ $$(e)\ a=5,b=9,c=-1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-9\pm\sqrt{101}}{10}\Rightarrow x\approx0.105,-1.90.$$ $$(f)\ a=2,b=-3,c=-18\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{153}}{4}\Rightarrow x\approx3.84,-2.34.$$ $$(g)\ 3x^{2}-16x+8=0,\ a=3,b=-16,c=8\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{16\pm\sqrt{160}}{6}\Rightarrow x\approx4.77,0.559.$$ $$(h)\ 3x^{2}-11x-18=0,\ a=3,b=-11,c=-18\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{11\pm\sqrt{337}}{6}\Rightarrow x\approx4.89,-1.23.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Multiply both sides by $$195x(x+2)$$ → $$195(x+2)+195x=\!28x(x+2).$$ Simplify → $$390x+390=\!28x^2+56x\Rightarrow28x^2-334x-390=0.$$ Divide by 2 → $$14x^2-167x-195=0.$$ Use the quadratic formula: $$x=\frac{167\pm\sqrt{167^2-4(14)(-195)}}{28}=\frac{167\pm\sqrt{34369}}{28}\approx\frac{167\pm185.3}{28}.$$ Hence $$x\approx12.6\text{ or }x\approx-0.65.$$ Since $x$ is positive, $$x\approx12.6.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Show that solving $$x^2 + 2bx + c = 0$$ by completing the square gives $$x = -b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - c}.$$
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: $$x^2 + 2bx = -c \Rightarrow (x + b)^2 - b^2 = -c \Rightarrow (x + b)^2 = b^2 - c \Rightarrow x + b = \pm \sqrt{b^2 - c} \Rightarrow x = -b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - c}.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Since $$(x-1)^2\ge0,$$ we have $$f(x)=(x-1)^2+1\ge1.$$ Equality when $$x=1,$$ so $$\min f(x)=1\ \text{at}\ x=1.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: $$3^x=1\Rightarrow x=0;\qquad 3^x=27=3^3\Rightarrow x=3.$$ Hence the roots are $$x=0,\ 3.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=x^2-6x+8$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,8),\ x\text{-ints from }(x-2)(x-4)=0\Rightarrow(2,0),(4,0).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=\frac{6}{2}=3,\ y_v=3^2-6\cdot3+8=-1\Rightarrow(3,-1).$$ Line of symmetry: $$x=3.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,25),\ x\text{-ints from }25-x^2=0\Rightarrow x=\pm5\Rightarrow(-5,0),(5,0).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=0,\ y_v=25\Rightarrow(0,25).$$ Axis: $$x=0.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=x^2+3x+2$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Sketch $$y=-x^2+6x+7$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,7),\ x\text{-ints from }-x^2+6x+7=0\Rightarrow x^2-6x-7=0\Rightarrow x=-1,7\Rightarrow(-1,0),(7,0).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=-\frac{6}{2(-1)}=3,\ y_v=-(3)^2+6(3)+7=16\Rightarrow(3,16).$$ Axis: $$x=3.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=2x^2+4x+10$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.

Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Quadratic formula for roots; vertex via $$-b/(2a)$$.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,10),\ x\text{-ints from }6x^2-19x+10=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{2}{3},\ \tfrac{5}{2}\Rightarrow\left(\tfrac{2}{3},0\right),\left(\tfrac{5}{2},0\right).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=\frac{19}{12},\ y_v=6\left(\tfrac{19}{12}\right)^2-19\left(\tfrac{19}{12}\right)+10=-\tfrac{121}{24}\Rightarrow\left(\tfrac{19}{12},-\tfrac{121}{24}\right).$$ Axis: $$x=\tfrac{19}{12}.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Sketch $$y=4-7x-2x^2$$: show intercepts, turning point, and line of symmetry.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Intercepts: $$y\text{-int }(0,4),\ x\text{-ints from }-2x^2-7x+4=0\Rightarrow2x^2+7x-4=0\Rightarrow x=-4,\ \tfrac{1}{2}\Rightarrow(-4,0),\left(\tfrac{1}{2},0\right).$$ Vertex: $$x_v=-\frac{-7}{2(-2)}=-\tfrac{7}{4},\ y_v=-2\left(-\tfrac{7}{4}\right)^2-7\left(-\tfrac{7}{4}\right)+4=\tfrac{81}{8}\Rightarrow\left(-\tfrac{7}{4},\tfrac{81}{8}\right).$$ Axis: $$x=-\tfrac{7}{4}.$$

Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Since $$\Delta=k^2+16\ge16>0$$ for all $$k\in\mathbb R,$$ the equation always has **two distinct real roots**.

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: (a) A car model is $$y=-0.01x^2+0.975x+16\ (x>0)$$ mpg. Find the two speeds at which $$y=32.5$$ mpg.
( b) Rewrite $$y=-0.01x^2+0.975x+16$$ in the form $$A-B(x-C)^2$$ and state $$A,B,C$$.
(c) Using the form in part (b), find the speed with greatest fuel efficiency.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Maximum at the vertex of a downward parabola.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Since $$y=A-B(x-C)^2$$ with $$B>0,$$ the maximum occurs at $$x=C=48.75\text{ mph}$$ (max mpg $$=A=39.765625$$).

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Use the model to find fuel consumption at $$x=120$$ mph and comment on validity at very high speeds.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: $$y=-0.01(120)^2+0.975(120)+16=-144+117+16=-11\text{ mpg}.$$ A negative mpg is not physically meaningful ⇒ the quadratic model is unreliable at very high speeds; it is valid only over a moderate speed range.

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: (a) A fertiliser model $$g=6+0.03f-0.00006f^2$$ (tonnes/ha) gives yield for fertiliser $$f$$ (kg/ha). According to the model, how much grain per hectare with no fertiliser?
(b) One farmer currently uses $$f=20$$ kg/ha. How much **additional** fertiliser is needed to increase yield by 1 tonne/ha?
Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Target $$g=6.576+1=7.576$$; solve for $$f$$ and choose the realistic root.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Current $$g(20)=6+0.03(20)-0.00006(20)^2=6.576.$$ Solve $$6+0.03f-0.00006f^2=7.576\Rightarrow -0.00006f^2+0.03f-1.576=0$$ ⇒ $$f\approx59.65\text{ or }440.35.$$ The realistic choice near 20 is $$f\approx59.65,$$ so **additional** fertiliser $$\approx59.65-20=39.65\text{ kg/ha}$$ (≈$$39.6$$ kg/ha).

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: A football stadium has 25,000 seats. The football club knows from experience that they will sell 10,000 tickets if each ticket costs £30. They also expect to sell 1,000 more tickets for every £1 the price decreases. (a) The number of tickets sold, $$t$$, can be modelled by the linear equation $$t=M-1000p$$, where £$$p$$ is the price of each ticket and $$M$$ is a constant. Find the value of $$M$$.

(b) The total revenue (£$$r$$) can be calculated by multiplying the number of tickets sold by the price of each ticket. This gives $$r=p(M-1000p)$$. Rewrite this in the form $$A-B(p-C)^2,$$ where $$A,B,C$$ are constants to be found.
(c) Using the revenue equation or otherwise, determine how much the football club should charge per ticket to make the maximum amount of money.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Maximum occurs at the vertex when $$p=C$$.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: From $$r=400000-1000(p-20)^2,$$ the maximum occurs at $$p=20.$$ Therefore, the club should charge **£20 per ticket** for maximum revenue.

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Lynn sold 80 cushions at £15 each. She expects to sell 10 more cushions for every £1 the price decreases. (a) The number sold is modelled by $$c=230-Hp$$ where £$$p$$ is the price and $$H$$ is a constant. Determine $$H$$.

Chapter 2-Quadratics.question_text: Lynn’s revenue is $$r=p(230-Hp)$$. Using $$H=10$$, (b) rewrite in the form $$A-B(p-C)^2$$ and state $$A,B,C$$.
(c) Using the form in part (b) or otherwise, show Lynn can increase revenue by £122.50 by lowering the price, and state the optimum selling price.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.hint: Compare current revenue with the vertex value.
Chapter 2-Quadratics.solution_text: Current revenue at £15: $$r_0=15\times80=1200.$$ From $$r=1322.5-10(p-11.5)^2,$$ maximum revenue is $$A=1322.5$$ at $$p=C=11.5.$$ Increase: $$1322.5-1200=£122.5.$$ Therefore, lowering the price to **£11.50** maximises revenue and increases it by **£122.50**.
